name: Battle of Königgrätz
info: On 3 July 1866 the Prussian armies defeated the Austrian army of Ludwig von Benedek near Königgrätz in Bohemia, the decisive battle of the Austro-Prussian War, which cleared the way for a German state without Austria.

facts.place: Near the Bohemian city of Hradec Králové (Königgrätz) and the village of Sadová, between the Bystřice and the Elbe, now in the Czech Republic
facts.sides: The Kingdom of Prussia under King Wilhelm I, with the Army of the Elbe (39,000) under Herwarth von Bittenfeld, the First Army (85,000) under Prince Friedrich Karl and the Second Army (almost 100,000) under Crown Prince Frederick William, against the Austrian Empire and its Saxon allies under Ludwig von Benedek, 215,000 men in the battle
facts.outcome: The Austrian army was forced to retreat across the Elbe with roughly 31,000 men killed, wounded or missing, against nearly 9,000 on the Prussian side. Prussia went on to win the war.

t: It was the single largest battle of the war and the largest in the world since Leipzig in 1813, with around 285,000 Prussian troops against 240,000 Austrians on the Bohemian front.

Almost all the fighting on the Prussian side was done by the First Army and one guards division of the Second, and the Prussian needle gun, a breechloader, outpaced the Austrian muzzleloaders in rate of fire.
The Prussian victory cleared a path to German unification without Austria and left Prussia a free hand when war with France came in 1870.
dyk: Austria had refused to sign the First Geneva Convention, so its medical personnel counted as combatants and withdrew with the army, leaving the wounded on the field. Over 900 lay without care until the Saxon nurse Marie Simon arrived several days later.
ev: The Army of the Elbe advances to Dresden and defeats the Saxon army of 23,000
Benedek reluctantly moves his army out of Olmütz
Moltke orders the First and Second Armies to Jitschin
Prince Friedrich Karl defeats the Austrian I Corps at Jitschin
The Prussian armies defeat Benedek's army between Sadová and Königgrätz
The last skirmish is fought at Blumenau as the Peace of Prague is being signed
The French ambassador presents Bismarck with a demand to relinquish Mainz
War with France, in whose background lay the French demand for revenge for Sadová

sections.background:
At the outset of the war in June 1866 the Prussian armies were gathered along the Prussian border: the Army of the Elbe under Karl Herwarth von Bittenfeld at Torgau, the First Army under Prince Friedrich Karl of Prussia between Senftenberg and Görlitz, and the Second Army under Crown Prince Frederick William in Silesia west of Neiße (Nysa). The Austrian army under Ludwig von Benedek was concentrated at Olmütz (Olomouc). The campaign began with Herwarth von Bittenfeld's advance to Dresden in the Kingdom of Saxony, where he easily defeated the Saxon army of 23,000 and joined with the First Army.

Benedek moved his troops out of Olmütz only reluctantly, on 18 June, marching north in three parallel columns with the I Corps protecting the right flank. On 22 June Helmuth von Moltke, Prussia's Chief of the General Staff, ordered both armies under his command to Jitschin (Jičín) near the Austrian positions, a daring manoeuvre undertaken to limit the war's duration despite the risk of one army being overtaken on the way.

Benedek was indecisive and failed to use his superior numbers to eliminate the Prussian armies one at a time. The Austrians were pressed back everywhere except at Trautenau (Trutnov), where they bested the Prussians despite great losses of their own. By 29 June Prince Friedrich Karl had reached Jitschin and inflicted a severe defeat on the Austrian I Corps under General Clam-Gallas, and the Crown Prince had reached Königinhof (Dvůr Králové) despite stiff resistance.
sections.forces:
Prussian forces totalled around 285,000 troops, whilst Austria had 240,000 men on the Bohemian front. Benedek had accepted the post of commander-in-chief with reluctance because he was unfamiliar with both the troops and the local terrain. On 3 July the Austrian army of 215,000 faced the Prussian Army of the Elbe (39,000) and First Army (85,000); the Second Army under the Crown Prince, almost 100,000 men, was still on the march.

The Prussian side had superior training, Moltke's tactical doctrine and the Dreyse needle gun, a breechloader with a far higher rate of fire than the Austrian muzzleloading small arms and cannon. It could be fired while prone and while moving quickly, whereas the Austrians had to stand up after each shot to reload their Lorenz rifles. The Prussians also made full use of railway transport, an innovation in European warfare. The Austrians relied heavily on the bayonet charge. Their artillery had the longer range, and their cavalry was thought to be the better.

The Austrian infantry was partially fortified on hilly, wooded ground, with cavalry in the rear and artillery covering the approaches. Benedek drew his army up against the Elbe between Sadová and Königgrätz, with the Saxons on the Austrian left. The Prussians took position west of the Bystřice river. Moltke had ordered the Second Army to join the others where the Austrians were assembled, but the telegraph lines to it were out, and two mounted officers rode the 32 kilometres to deliver the order at 4 am.
sections.course:
The battle began at dawn in subsiding rain and mist. Shortly before 8 am the Austrian artillery opened fire, pinning down the Prussian right flank under Herwarth von Bittenfeld, while the Saxons on the Austrian left fired on the Prussian right from higher ground. In the centre the Prussian 7th Division under General Fransecky led the advance into the Swiepwald, where it met two Austrian corps, and King Wilhelm I ordered the First Army across the river to support it. A fierce fight followed in the forest. Austrian artillery fired into the smoke of the Prussian advance and cut down the 8th and 4th Divisions as they emerged from it. Benedek refused to call for a cavalry charge, which later commentators have argued might have won the battle.

At 11 am the Austrian centre moved to flank the 7th Division. Colonel Carl von Pöckh drove it back to the edge of the forest with an infantry charge, but flanking fire from the 8th Division destroyed his battalion as a fighting force and killed him. Close fighting in the forest negated Austrian advantages, as the artillery could not be trained on it and the IV Corps was committed piecemeal.

At 2:30 pm the Crown Prince arrived with almost 100,000 men and hit the Austrian right flank. The 1st Prussian Guard under Hiller von Gaertringen reached the Austrian artillery, the Second Army broke through and took Chlum behind the centre and the Army of the Elbe broke through the left. Benedek ordered a general retreat and cavalry countercharges to cover it. They kept the bridges over the Elbe open and prevented pursuit, but 2,000 men and almost as many horses were killed, wounded or captured. Benedek crossed the Elbe near 6 pm.
sections.aftermath:
The battle ended with heavy casualties for both sides. The Prussians had nearly 9,000 men killed, wounded or missing. The Austrians and their allies had roughly 31,000 men killed, wounded or missing, 9,291 of them prisoners, and lost 187 cannon and 51 colours. Austria had earlier refused to sign the First Geneva Convention, so its medical personnel were regarded as combatants and withdrew with the main body of the forces, leaving the wounded to die on the field. Over 900 soldiers lay wounded without medical care until the Saxon nurse Marie Simon arrived several days later with a large stock of supplies and tended them for 17 weeks. This experience led her and Carola of Vasa to establish the Albert Association, a precursor to the German Red Cross.

Dismayed by his earlier losses, Benedek had urged Emperor Franz Josef to make peace as the only way to save the army from a catastrophe. That evening he informed the emperor that the catastrophe had occurred. The Prussians pursued the Austrian Nord-Armee and fought a series of minor clashes, the last at Blumenau (today's Lamač, district of Bratislava, Slovakia) on 22 July, just as the Peace of Prague was being signed.

After the victory France attempted to extract territorial concessions in the Palatinate and Luxembourg. Bismarck told the Reichstag on 2 May 1871 that on 6 August 1866 the French ambassador had presented what he called, to put it succinctly, an ultimatum: to relinquish Mainz or expect an immediate declaration of war.
sections.sources:
The battle is known above all through the movements and losses recorded for the armies. The decision to stand at the Elbe turned on a telegram: when Franz Josef refused Benedek's request for peace, an ambiguous last sentence of the imperial telegram was interpreted as ordering a final stand. Bismarck's speech to the Reichstag of 2 May 1871 records the French demand of August 1866.

Several points are argued over. Later commentators have argued that a cavalry charge ordered by Benedek might have won the battle. The Prussian artillery was ineffective, and almost all the fighting on the Prussian side was done by the First Army and one guards division of the Second. The battlefield holds 475 memorials, some at the places where individuals, mostly officers, were killed and others at the mass graves in which Austrian, Prussian and Saxon soldiers often rest together, put up with funds from families, regiments, officers, the Order of St. John and the Central Committee for the Preservation of Monuments from the War of 1866.
sections.legacy:
Königgrätz was the decisive battle of the Austro-Prussian War. It was the single largest battle of the war and the largest in the world since the Battle of Leipzig in 1813. The Prussian 7th Infantry Division and 1st Guards Infantry Division attacked and destroyed 38 out of 49 infantry battalions of four Austrian corps at the Swiepwald and at Chlum, and the Austrian army was forced to retreat at 3 pm, before any Prussian reinforcements could engage its flanks.

The victory gave Prussian statesmen a great opportunity. It cleared a path toward German unification, in particular with the Little Germany solution, Germany without Austria, and the subsequent foundation of the North German Confederation. It also ensured that Prussia would have a free hand when a war with France came to pass in 1870. The French public resented the Prussian victory and demanded Revanche pour Sadova, revenge for Sadová, which formed part of the background to the Franco-Prussian War.

The Königgrätzer Marsch was written to commemorate the battle, and the memorials on the field and in its surroundings number 475. The experience of the wounded left on the field led Marie Simon and Carola of Vasa to found the Albert Association, a precursor to the German Red Cross.

summary: At Königgrätz on 3 July 1866 the Prussian armies defeated the Austrian army of Ludwig von Benedek, the largest battle of the Austro-Prussian War. It cleared the way for a German state without Austria and left Prussia a free hand against France in 1870.

notes: Garbled in the article: 'the fortress Josefstadt was concentrated at' (left out); 'Karl Eberhard Herwarth von Bittenfeld' in the Austrian counterattack section is probably Herwarth von Bittenfeld again (not used).

Timing disagrees: the lead and the Second Army section put the Austrian retreat at 3 pm, the same section has Benedek ordering withdrawal by 4 pm after the Second Army arrived at 2:30 pm. I give 3 pm only in the legacy section, as the lead does, and no time in the course.

Strengths: 285,000 and 240,000 (whole front) against 215,000 vs 39,000 plus 85,000 on the day; the Second Army (almost 100,000) arrived later. The 215,000 is not the Austrian total with allies explicitly.
The lead says the Prussian artillery was ineffective, while the text says its shorter range was moot; I used the lead's statement in sources only.
The article gives no named historical sources for the battle; the sources section is thin and turns to what is argued (the cavalry charge, the telegram) and to the memorials.
Left out: the Bismarck quotation in full, the claim that the 7th Division held off nearly a quarter of the Austrian army, artillery details (66 guns under Rozynski).
